summary: OpenJLPT's grammar is indeed unusable (exactly 20 points per level, 100 total — I confirmed by counting). But a single, complete, reusable, CC-licensed replacement DOES exist, so you do not need me to hand-enumerate the list. tristcoil/hanabira.org-japanese-content ships 5 flat JSON files covering 828 grammar points (N5 136 / N4 124 / N3 132 / N2 191 / N1 245), every one with an English short + long explanation, a formation string and 4 example sentences (jp/romaji/en) — zero empty fields across all 828. gokan-dev/gokan-dataset is a build-time enrichment of that same corpus: 755 of those points re-published with examples already kuromoji-tokenized, each token carrying a JMdict vocabId, plus patternWordIndices marking the grammar marker inside each sentence (3,020 of 3,040 examples), a construction/inflection classification, a conjugations.json drill table, and 84 named near-synonym families with register notes. I built and ran the merge: 828 points, 756 enriched (91.3%), 3,024 cloze-ready examples, 2.8MB raw / 537KB gzipped total, 70-174KB gzipped per level. Those two datasets alone deliver the grammar lesson page, the auto-generated exercises, the "similar but different" contrasts, and the tap-any-word feature — all offline, all built at build time.

recommendations.title: Grammar spine = hanabira 828 points, enriched by gokan; delete OpenJLPT grammar entirely
recommendations.decision: Build-time: fetch the 5 hanabira JSON files (1.2MB total) as the canonical per-level list, then sparse-clone gokan-dataset's compiled/grammar (4.8MB, 5.6s, 755 point files + index/ + conjugations.json) and left-join by normalized title. Normalization that works: NFKC, strip the trailing romaji parenthetical, strip all whitespace, map the wave dash variants together. Ship one file per level: data/grammar/n5.json … n1.json. Keep OpenJLPT for vocab (8,334) and kanji (2,211) only — its grammar files are 20 items each and must not be shipped.
recommendations.why: Verified by running it: hanabira N5 136 / N4 124 / N3 132 / N2 191 / N1 245 = 828, all fields populated, 4 examples each. Join rate 132/136, 115/124, 115/132, 170/191, 224/245 = 756 matched, 72 fall back to plain-but-complete hanabira data. OpenJLPT grammar counted: exactly 20 per level. 828 sits between JLPT Sensei's 848 and Bunpro's 945, i.e. it is a real-world-complete list, not a sample.

recommendations.title: Generate every grammar exercise from the data instead of authoring questions
recommendations.decision: Four generators, each keyed off a field that already exists: (1) CLOZE — blank the tokens at example.patternWordIndices; only run on kind==='construction' (741 of 755 points, 3,024 examples have non-empty indices). (2) TRANSFORM — for kind==='inflection' (14 points), read compiled/grammar/conjugations.json which already gives {lemma, lemmaReading, target, targetReading, wordClass:'godan'|'ichidan'|'irregular'} lists. (3) PICK-THE-PARTICLE — blank any token whose surface is in a particle set and whose vocabId is null; distractors from the same set. (4) SENTENCE-ORDERING — shuffle example.words[] (they concatenate back to jp exactly, so reassembly validation is free). Distractors for cloze come from the point's family.relatedPoints — those are near-synonyms, so they are genuinely hard, not random.
recommendations.why: The gokan SCHEMA.md documents that `kind` exists precisely because inflection points cannot be cloze-tested: n5-046 (te-form) would blank a fixed kana instead of asking for the conjugation, and n1-178 (potential) is the only point in the corpus with no locatable pattern. I verified 741 construction / 14 inflection and 3,024/3,040 examples with usable patternWordIndices. Building the quiz off these fields means zero question authoring for 828 points.

recommendations.title: Grammar lesson page contract
recommendations.decision: One screen, in this order: (1) header — pattern in large type, romaji, level chip, formality chip (casual/neutral/polite/formal/very-formal-literary, present on 370 points); (2) one-line meaning (short_explanation); (3) FORMATION block rendered as a table by splitting the formation string on the separator characters — one row per attachment (Noun+no / Verb dictionary form / Verb ta-form); (4) long_explanation; (5) 4 example sentences rendered from words[] as tappable chips — pattern tokens highlighted, tokens with vocabId open the SAME vocab sheet the video subtitles use, with a Save button; (6) 'Easy to confuse with' — family.relatedPoints rendered as cards showing each sibling's usageNote (379 points have one) and family.axis (register / constraint / variant), which literally says what this member adds over its siblings; (7) practice CTA; (8) source/attribution line. Add a 'common mistake' slot fed from JLPTSuccess for N5.
recommendations.why: Every field in that contract exists in the merged data — I did not invent any of it. The independently-built JLPTSuccess N5 corpus converged on almost the same schema (form_rules.conjugations, explanation_en, examples, common_mistakes, contrasts, politeness_ladder, wrong_corrected_pair, see_also), which is strong evidence this is the right page for a grammar point.

recommendations.title: Teach N5/N4 in Genki order, ship it as an explicit `unit` field — never alphabetical
recommendations.decision: hanabira is sorted alphabetically by romaji, which is useless for learning. Add a build-time `unit` and `unitOrder` to each N5/N4 point using the 12+10 unit sequence in code_or_data. Level home screen shows Units ('Introduce yourself', 'Numbers and time', …) as the primary path, with the full A-Z list behind a 'Browse all' tab for lookup. A learner finishing N5 Unit 5 can already self-introduce, ask where things are, say what they did yesterday, and invite someone out — that is the 'speak fast' the user asked for.
recommendations.why: Not invented: gauravhq/JLPTSuccess's N5 corpus carries genki_lesson {book,lesson} on 178/178 points and minna_chapter on 175/178, and I dumped the full Genki-ordered grouping (Genki I L1: desu/wa/ga/no/nani/nanji…; L6: te-form, te kudasai, te mo ii, te wa ikemasen; L9: plain past, relative clauses). The units below are that real textbook sequence, regrouped. Genki I ≈ N5, Genki II ≈ N4, which also matches Minna no Nihongo 1-25 / 26-50.

recommendations.title: One SRS queue for vocab, kanji AND grammar — item type is just a field
recommendations.decision: Store every reviewable as {id, type:'vocab'|'kanji'|'grammar', srs:{due, stability, difficulty, reps, lapses, state}}. Use FSRS-4.5/5 (a ~100-line pure-JS scheduler, no dependency) rather than SM-2; on a grammar item the 'front' rotates between the four generators above so the same point is not always the same question. A saved word from a video subtitle and a grammar point failed in a quiz land in the same 'Due today' count on the home screen. Persist in IndexedDB, never localStorage, and keep the review log as an append-only array so the schedule can be recomputed if you change algorithms.
recommendations.why: The user asked to save words and review them as flashcards; grammar retention fails for exactly the same reason vocabulary does, and Bunpro's whole product is grammar-in-an-SRS. Keeping one queue means one streak, one daily number, one habit loop — two separate queues is the classic reason these apps get abandoned. Append-only logs are what let Anki/FSRS re-derive schedules after an algorithm change.

recommendations.title: Use the same word-tap sheet everywhere: grammar examples, story text, and video subtitles
recommendations.decision: Build one component, openWordSheet(vocabId | surface). gokan's grammar examples already resolve 10,989 of 33,316 tokens (33%) to a JMdict vocabId; for the unresolved 67% (particles, names, rare forms) fall back to a build-time lookup table keyed by surface form built from jmdict-eng-common, then to the online jisho.org API when the phone has network. The sheet shows reading, meanings, JLPT level, the sentence it came from, and one Save button that writes straight into the SRS queue.
recommendations.why: The user's headline feature is 'press any Japanese word, get an explanation, save it for later'. Since gokan already ships the tokenization with vocab ids, the same renderer that makes a grammar example tappable makes a subtitle line tappable — you write the hard part (tokenization) zero times at runtime. Doing it as one component also means one visual language across the app.

recommendations.title: Add a build-time contrast/confusion drill mode from the 84 families
recommendations.decision: Ship compiled/grammar/index/families.json as its own data file and add a 'Confusing pairs' drill per level: present a sentence, ask which family member fits. The big families are worth dedicated lessons: causality 16 members (kara/node/tame/okage de/sei de…), contradiction 13, regardless-whether-A-or-B 12, concession 12, inference 11, exclusivity 9. Filter members to the learner's level and one level above.
recommendations.why: Verified: 84 families, 370 points carry one, family.relatedPoints is derived at build time so it is symmetric and complete, and family.axis tags whether a sibling differs by register, constraint or variant. 'Similar but different points to contrast' was an explicit design requirement and this is it, pre-computed. Distinguishing kara vs node vs tame ni is exactly where N3/N2 learners lose exam points.

recommendations.title: Pull JLPTSuccess N5 in as a second, richer layer for the first level only
recommendations.decision: For N5 only, join gauravhq/JLPTSuccess N5/data/grammar.json (178 patterns, 3.3MB, CC BY-SA 4.0) on pattern and lift three fields the other sources lack: common_mistakes [{wrong, right, why, category}], wrong_corrected_pair, and politeness_ladder {casual/polite/humble/respectful}. Render common_mistakes as a red/green 'Don't say this / Say this' card. Do NOT use its N4 file — I checked, N4/data/grammar.json is a 128-pattern skeleton with every explanation, example, mistake and contrast array empty.
recommendations.why: N5 is where the user starts and where wrong habits calcify, and this is the only dataset I found with authored wrong/right pairs (e.g. 'watashi wa gakusei desu ja arimasen' -> 'watashi wa gakusei ja arimasen', 'don't combine desu and ja arimasen'). It also carries genki_lesson/minna_chapter on all 178, which is the source of the teaching order. Its own _meta admits the 'native review' was done by an LLM in a reviewer persona, so treat it as a helpful extra layer over hanabira, not a replacement.

recommendations.title: Honour the licences in the app, and keep three tempting sources out
recommendations.decision: hanabira requires a visible link back to hanabira.org; gokan and JLPTSuccess content are CC BY-SA 4.0, so the app's content is CC BY-SA 4.0 too and a Sources/Licences screen must list hanabira.org, gokan-dataset, JLPTSuccess, EDRDG/JMdict, Tatoeba and OpenJLPT. Exclude: (a) bee-san/bees-ultimate-grammar-dictionary — its 12 sources are DoJG, HJGP, Donna Toki, Bunpro etc., and only the NINJAL+Yokubi public build is redistributable (473KB zip, 1,550 entries, no JLPT level tags, Japanese-only structured content — wrong shape anyway); (b) mxggle/anki-jlpt-n2-grammar-example-sentences — CC BY-NC 4.0 and a direct transcription of the copyrighted Shin Kanzen Master N2 textbook; (c) scraping Bunpro or JLPT Sensei.
recommendations.why: Verified each: I downloaded the bee-san public zip and counted 1,550 entries with no level tag; mxggle's notes.json is 531 sentences straight out of the textbook with Chinese translations. A phone app the user installs is a distribution, so NC and textbook-derived content are real exposure, and the CC BY-SA on hanabira/gokan is viral over the content bundle.

recommendations.title: Professional/business Japanese is a separate track, not just N2+N1 grammar
recommendations.decision: After N4 Unit 10 (keigo basics) unlock a 'Work Japanese' track built from: the ~30 keigo points already in N4, the 52 gokan points tagged formalityLevel:'formal' (48 of them N2), plus a hand-authored set of ~40 workplace formulas that no JLPT list contains: telephone openers, email templates, cushion words, the request ladder (te kudasai < te itadakemasu ka < te itadakemasen deshou ka), uchi/soto in-group rules, and hou-ren-sou. Keep the 95 'very-formal-literary' points in a separate READING track.
recommendations.why: The user explicitly wants 'professional and work Japanese' after basics, and JLPT does not test it — JLPT rewards reading stiff written grammar. I checked the formality distribution: very-formal-literary is 95 points and 90 of them are N1 (katagata, zukume, taritomo ~nai) — literary/written forms for reading contracts and news, not things you say to a manager. Conflating the two would teach the wrong register.

recommendations.title: Ship grammar per level as separate lazy-loaded files, precache only N5
recommendations.decision: Service worker precaches the shell + n5.json (72KB gz); n4-n1 are cache-on-first-visit via a 'Download N3 (86KB)' button on the level card. Serve the JSON pre-gzipped and parse with JSON.parse of a fetched string, not an inline JS object literal.
recommendations.why: Measured on the real merged output: N5 410KB raw/72KB gz, N4 398/70, N3 442/86, N2 703/140, N1 897/174, total 2,851KB raw / 537KB gz. Small enough to ship everything, big enough that parsing all five on a phone at startup is a wasted second. iOS Safari also evicts large caches, so making the download explicit per level is honest about it.

recommendations.title: Keep jkindrix/japanese-language-data as the fallback/QA source, not the primary
recommendations.decision: Its grammar-curated/n{1..5}.json (595 points: N5 77 / N4 89 / N3 130 / N2 149 / N1 150, CC-BY-SA 4.0) has fields hanabira lacks — formation_notes[], formality, and a `related` array of point ids. Use it at build time as a cross-check: any point present there but missing from hanabira is a coverage gap worth a look, and its formation_notes can fill hanabira's formation string where that string is thin.
recommendations.why: Downloaded and inspected all five: entries are genuinely well-written (the desu entry explains it is the polite form of da, does not conjugate like a verb, gives the plain equivalent and the feminine drop). But every single one of the 595 is review_status:'draft' with sources:'General Japanese grammar knowledge', i.e. unreviewed generated content, and 595 < 828, so it loses to hanabira on both volume and provenance.

verified_facts.claim: OpenJLPT's grammar files contain exactly 20 points per level (100 total) — far too thin, as suspected
verified_facts.evidence: curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evanclan/OpenJLPT/main/data/json/grammar/n{5,4,3,2,1}.json piped to len() -> n5 20, n4 20, n3 20, n2 20, n1 20

verified_facts.claim: tristcoil/hanabira.org-japanese-content ships a complete 828-point JLPT grammar corpus as 5 flat JSON files with English explanations and 4 examples each
verified_facts.evidence: HTTP 200 on https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tristcoil/hanabira.org-japanese-content/main/grammar_json/grammar_ja_{N5|N4|N3|N2|N1}_full_alphabetical_0001.json — sizes 179,611 / 172,030 / 196,588 / 300,563 / 370,544 bytes; counts N5 136, N4 124, N3 132, N2 191, N1 245 = 828. Fields: title, short_explanation, long_explanation, formation, examples[{jp,romaji,en}]. Examples-per-point: 4 for 827 points, 2 for one N4 point. Zero empty values across all five required fields at every level. Licence: Creative Commons, requires a link back to hanabira.org.

verified_facts.claim: gokan-dev/gokan-dataset republishes that corpus enriched with tokenized examples, JMdict word ids, pattern positions, families and conjugation drills
verified_facts.evidence: GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse then sparse-checkout set compiled/grammar -> 5.6s, 4.8MB, 755 point files + index/{jlpt,families}.json + conjugations.json. Per level: N5 132, N4 115, N3 113, N2 170, N1 225 = 755. 741 kind='construction', 14 kind='inflection'. 3,040 examples, 3,020 with non-empty patternWordIndices. 33,316 example tokens, 10,989 (33.0%) carrying a JMdict vocabId. 370 points with formalityLevel, 379 with usageNote, 370 with a family; 84 families, largest = causality (16 members). conjugations.json gives 14 transformation drill tables with lemma/target/reading/wordClass. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0, derived from hanabira + JMdict/EDRDG + Tatoeba.

verified_facts.claim: The hanabira + gokan merge works and produces a shippable payload — I built and ran it
verified_facts.evidence: Normalize title (NFKC, strip trailing romaji paren, strip whitespace, unify wave dash), join on (level, title): matched N5 132/136, N4 115/124, N3 115/132, N2 170/191, N1 224/245 = 756 of 828 (91.3%); the other 72 keep full hanabira content. Output 828 points, 3,024 cloze-ready examples, 3,141,385 bytes pretty / 2,851KB compact / 537KB gzipped; per level gzipped N5 72KB, N4 70KB, N3 86KB, N2 140KB, N1 174KB.

verified_facts.claim: gauravhq/JLPTSuccess has a genuinely rich N5 grammar corpus (178 patterns) but its N4 file is an empty skeleton
verified_facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gauravhq/JLPTSuccess/master/N5/data/grammar.json -> 200, 3,287,581 bytes, 178 patterns, 57 distinct fields incl. common_mistakes, contrasts, politeness_ladder, wrong_corrected_pair, genki_lesson (178/178 populated), minna_chapter (175/178), audio paths, pitch_marks. N4/data/grammar.json -> 200 but only 61,157 bytes / 128 patterns with examples=[], common_mistakes=[], contrasts=[], explanation_en='' on all 128. N3/N2/N1 -> 404. Content CC BY-SA 4.0, code MIT; its own _meta admits the 'native reviewer' pass was performed by an LLM in a reviewer persona.

verified_facts.claim: Canonical grammar-point counts per level differ a lot by reference — 828 is a defensible target
verified_facts.evidence: Bunpro live index (counted level:'JLPTn' occurrences in the embedded JSON on https://bunpro.jp/grammar_points): N5 132, N4 185, N3 220, N2 221, N1 187, plus 21 Kansai-ben = 945+. JLPT Sensei (page totals): N5 84, N4 132, N3 182, N2 197, N1 253 = 848. hanabira/gokan: 136/124/132/191/245 = 828. jkindrix: 77/89/130/149/150 = 595. muzuiyo db: N5 16, N4 66, N3 180, N2 173, N1 226 (+101 'N0'). Shin Kanzen Master N2 grammar: 138 distinct patterns over 26 lessons (counted from mxggle notes.json, 531 notes). Dictionary of Japanese Grammar: ~200 Basic / 196 Intermediate / ~200 Advanced, not JLPT-keyed. tanos.co.uk grammar pages now return HTTP 500 (site index 200, /jlpt/jlpt5/grammar/ and /jlpt4/ both 500) — dead as a source.

verified_facts.claim: bee-san/bees-ultimate-grammar-dictionary's public release is unusable for this app
verified_facts.evidence: Downloaded https://github.com/bee-san/bees-ultimate-grammar-dictionary/releases/download/v2026.09.09-public/bees-ultimate-grammar-dictionary.zip -> 200, 483,953 bytes, 5 members, 1,550 term_bank entries. Yomitan structured-content format, no JLPT level tags on any entry, index.json attribution = 'NINJAL + Yokubi, CC BY 4.0' only. Its SOURCES.md confirms the full 12-source build (DoJG, HJGP, Donna Toki, Bunpro, IMABI…) is personal-use only and not redistributable.

verified_facts.claim: mxggle N2 deck is high quality but licence-blocked
verified_facts.evidence: notes.json -> 200, 1,858,162 bytes, 531 notes over 26 lessons, 138 distinct grammarPattern values, fields incl. readingFurigana, grammarFormation, styleNotes, explanationJapanese, explanationChinese, audioFile. Licence CC BY-NC 4.0 and content is transcribed from the Shin Kanzen Master N2 grammar textbook. Useful only as an offline cross-check of the canonical N2 pattern list.

verified_facts.claim: The other candidate repos are dead ends
verified_facts.evidence: kananinirav/jlptbenkyo -> repo is 1KB, README only, links to the commercial jlptbenkyo.com site; no data. muzuiyo/jlptgrammar -> MIT, lib/assets/jlptgrammar.db is a 2.69MB SQLite with one table jlptgrammar(id, level, name, grammar, mean, example, notes), 762 rows, but 'mean' is Chinese and there are no English translations. Ralphbupt/japanese-grammar -> CC BY 4.0 but Japanese+Chinese markdown lessons N5-N2 only; grammar/N5/lesson00.md 404s, so the README's paths are stale. Bunpro has no public JSON API: /api/v3/grammar_points and /api/grammar_points.json both 404, /grammar_points.json 406.

risks: Both hanabira and gokan are CC BY-SA 4.0 / CC-with-attribution. That is viral over the content bundle: the app's grammar/vocab content must itself be CC BY-SA 4.0, and a Sources screen must link back to hanabira.org, gokan-dataset, EDRDG/JMdict and Tatoeba. Skipping the attribution screen is the single easiest licence breach here.

None of these grammar corpora are human-expert-reviewed. hanabira says 'proofreadings' in its changelog with no reviewer named; jkindrix marks all 595 entries review_status:'draft'; JLPTSuccess's own _meta admits its 'native reviewer' was an LLM in a reviewer persona. Expect occasional wrong nuance. Mitigate with a one-tap 'Report this explanation' button and a visible 'community-sourced, not textbook-verified' note - do not claim the content is authoritative.

Do not try to auto-generate the missing grammar points with an LLM to close the gap to Bunpro's 945. Invented grammar points are worse than a shorter list, and 828 is already a complete real-world level set.

The title join between hanabira and gokan is fuzzy. 72 of 828 points do not match because of parenthetical/whitespace/wave-dash differences. Do not drop unmatched points - fall back to the hanabira record (which is complete on its own) and mark enriched:false so the UI hides the tappable-token and cloze features for those 72.

Alphabetical order is the default in hanabira and it is a trap. If you ship the level as an A-Z list the user starts at 'A ga ichiban' (superlatives) instead of desu/wa, and quits. The unit order must be the default screen.

patternWordIndices is empty on 20 of 3,040 examples, and the schema documents one point (n1-178, the potential form) where the pattern is unlocatable in every example. Guard the cloze generator on a non-empty array or it will render a question with no blank.

Only 33% of example tokens resolve to a JMdict vocabId, so a tap on a particle or a rare conjugated form returns nothing. Build a surface-form fallback table at build time from jmdict-eng-common and show 'no entry - search online' rather than an empty sheet, or the headline tap-any-word feature will feel broken.

bee-san's full 12-source dictionary and the mxggle N2 deck are the two most tempting datasets and both are legally unusable in a distributed app (copyrighted textbook content / CC BY-NC). 'It's just for me' stops being true the moment the PWA is hosted at a URL.

JLPTSuccess N5's audio paths (audio/grammar/n5-001.0.mp3) and pitch_marks reference files in that repo, not yours. If you lift those fields, either fetch the audio at build time (check size first - the repo is 264MB) or strip the audio references so the UI does not render dead play buttons.

gokan is a small project (one maintainer, git-LFS raw data) and hanabira is a hobby portal. Vendor the JSON into your repo at build time - do not fetch from raw.githubusercontent.com at runtime. The offline requirement and CORS both make runtime fetching wrong anyway.

GitHub's unauthenticated API rate limit (60/hr) is hit quickly while exploring - I hit it mid-research. The build pipeline must use raw.githubusercontent.com and git clone, never api.github.com, or CI will fail intermittently.
